sections.title: Where does a plant's energy come from?

components.content_intent: Open with the windowsill plant and surface the soil-food idea without resolving it yet.

sections.title: Light to chemical energy
sections.transition_note: After the hook, name the conversion: light energy becomes chemical energy in glucose.

components.content_intent: State that photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose; exclude soil-as-food.
Define photosynthesis with inputs (light, water, CO2) and output (glucose + oxygen).

sections.title: Trace the windowsill example
sections.transition_note: Apply the definition to the same windowsill plant step by step.

components.content_intent: Walk the windowsill plant through light → chlorophyll → glucose, contrasting soil nutrients vs food energy.

sections.title: Practice the conversion story
sections.transition_note: Learners try the conversion story on a new plant context after the model.

components.content_intent: Prompt learners to explain energy conversion for a shaded vs sunny plant without inventing new science.

sections.title: Check understanding
sections.transition_note: Close with a check that targets M1 soil-food and M2 breathing-opposite ideas.

components.content_intent: Ask one check that forces a choice between soil-food and light-to-glucose conversion.

card_rubrics.objective: Explain that plants convert light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose.

misconceptions.description: Plants get their food by absorbing nutrients from soil.
Photosynthesis is just the opposite of breathing / animals breathe out what plants breathe in.
